answer:
From the Antoine equation, water's vapour pressure at 180 °C is about **9.97 bar (0.997 MPa, 7,480 mmHg)**. The IAPWS-IF97 steam tables give 10.03 bar, so this is about 0.5% low. I ran all three calculations below in Python.

**Constants used:** the standard high-temperature set for water, valid from 99 to 374 °C. Pressure P is in mmHg and temperature T in °C.

log10 P = A − B / (C + T), with A = 8.14019, B = 1810.94, C = 244.485

- P = 10^(8.14019 − 1810.94 / 424.485) ≈ 7,480 mmHg ≈ 9.97 bar

**Which constants you use matters:**

| Method | Pressure at 180 °C | Compared with steam tables |
|---|---|---|
| Antoine, high-temperature set (99–374 °C) | 9.97 bar | −0.5% |
| Antoine, NIST Bridgeman–Aldrich set (A = 3.55959, B = 643.748, C = −198.043; P in bar, T in K; valid 379–573 K) | 10.87 bar | +8% |
| IAPWS-IF97 steam tables (`iapws` package) | 10.03 bar | reference |

Use the first set: its stated range covers 180 °C and it agrees with the steam tables. The NIST set is off by 8% at this temperature, even though 453 K is inside the range it is listed for. The common 1–100 °C constants (A = 8.07131, B = 1730.63, C = 233.426) are not valid at 180 °C.
